title: ATD 2026: Hallway chats, cheaper failures and bending systems
author: Jit Gosai
text: I’ve been at Agile Testing Days (ATD) for the last four days, and what a ride! They pretty much take over the hotel in Potsdam, Germany, with speakers, attendees and organisers all packed into the venue. From around 8am till 11pm, there’s something going on. Yoga, breakfast, Lean Coffee, games, hallway conversations, panel discussions, and that’s before you even get into the talks and workshops. Hallway chats I spent a lot of time diving in and out of talks and chatting with folks. Honestly, these are some of the best parts of conferences. If you’ve got something bouncing around your head and want to get other people’s opinions, this is where to do it. Now I’m pretty lucky. Having spoken at conferences over the years, I’ve made friends with lots of people, so sitting down to pick their brains is much easier for me. But I’d still encourage you to speak to the speakers. If they’re hanging around the public spaces, chances are they’re happy to chat. Just smile, introduce yourself and dive in. If you saw their talk, share something you liked or, even better, something you took away from it. Trust me , they’ll love that! I spent a lot of time simply asking, “Hey, would you be up for a chat? I’d love to get your take on something.” Another great question was “Who else should I speak to?” Often they’d suggest someone else, and if I didn’t know them, I’d ask for an introduction. Before you know it, you’re slowly building out your network. A few ATD 2026 takeaways So what am I taking away from ATD this year? Here are four ideas that are still bouncing around my head. Making failure cheap - Clare Norman I shared a little of Clare’s opening keynote on Notes , but something really connected with my learning from failure series. How do we make failure cheaper so we can learn from it rather than just trying to prevent it? But Clare helped me see something I’d not really considered. A failure doesn’t cost everyone the same. Think about a reminder feature. Forgetting to take out your bins isn’t the end of the world, but missing a reminder to take your medication could have much more serious consequences. So when we’re making failure cheap, we need to think about who is actually paying the cost. If you watch any talk from ATD, then I’d highly recommend this one . So many of Clare’s ideas connect to quality engineering. Levers, signals and noise - Elisabeth Hendrickson and Joel Tosi I loved this framing. Levers are things within a system we can influence or change, while signals are observable changes that tell us something meaningful is happening. I often shortcut signals to feedback, but I like this framing better. It makes me think more carefully about what we’re observing and whether it’s actually telling us anything useful. This connected closely with my talk on sociotechnical systems. If we want to change how our systems behave, we need to understand which levers we can pull and what signals might tell us whether we’re making a difference. And, importantly, how do we distinguish those signals from noise? Elisabeth and Joel have also written a book on this, Signals & Levers , which is going on my reading list! Bend the system - Anne-Marie Charrett Anne-Marie gave me such a simple idea that had never really occurred to me before. We’re regularly told we need to change the system. I’ve probably said it countless times myself. But what if changing the system isn’t possible, at least not right now? Why not try bending it instead? Shift the language, tweak a default approach, build on existing momentum or make the right things the easy things. Small nudges might not give us the change we’re looking for immediately, but they could start moving things in the right direction. I really like this idea, especially when thinking about long-term culture change. Anne-Marie also has a new book out - The Quality Coach’s Handbook . title: Charakterystyki jakości AI
text: Jeśli chcecie przypomnieć sobie, jak wygląda przegląd charakterystyk i podcharakterystyk, sięgnijcie po ISO/IEC 25010. To międzynarodowa norma definiująca model jakości oprogramowania oraz systemów. Określa ona, jakie cechy decydują o tym, że dany produkt informatyczny jest wysokiej jakości. Stanowi uniwersalny punkt odniesienia przy projektowaniu, analizie oraz testowaniu oprogramowania (m.in. w sylabusach ISTQB®). Model ten można zwizualizować następująco: Jeśli chcecie poznać je bliżej, to zachęcamy do zapoznania się z opracowaniem Adama Romana w tym zakresie: https://pqb.org.pl/documents/Model-ISO-25010-PL-v1.0.pdf Standard ISO/IEC 25059 przynosi nam dodatkowe charakterystyki specyficzne dla sztucznej inteligencji. Jest to międzynarodowy standard o nazwie Software engineering – Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) – Quality model for AI systems, który został opublikowany w czerwcu 2023 roku przez ISO oraz IEC. Stanowi rozszerzenie popularnej serii standardów SQuaRE (w szczególności ISO/IEC 25010). Tradycyjne modele jakości oprogramowania zakładały determinizm (ten sam input daje zawsze taki sam, w 100% poprawny output). Systemy oparte na sztucznej inteligencji i uczeniu maszynowym (ML) działają inaczej – generują wyniki probabilistyczne (oparte na prawdopodobieństwie), uczą się na danych i mogą wykazywać zmienność zachowań. ISO/IEC 25059 ma na celu ujednolicenie tego, jak mierzyć, oceniać i specyfikować jakość takich systemów. Standard rozszerza model jakości o nowe podcechy i modyfikuje istniejące definicje: - Poprawność funkcjonalna (Functional correctness): zmodyfikowana pod kątem tego, że systemy AI nie zawsze gwarantują pełną poprawność we wszystkich obserwowanych warunkach. - Kontrola ze strony użytkownika (User controllability): możliwość terminowej interwencji człowieka lub agenta. - Adaptacyjność funkcjonalna (Functional adaptability): zdolność systemu do nabywania i wykorzystywania danych do przewidywania. - Odporność (Robustness): utrzymanie poprawności działania w przypadku danych nieoczekiwanych lub adwersarialnych (ataków na AI). - Przejrzystość (Transparency): komunikowanie informacji o działaniu systemu. - Interweniowalność (Intervenability): zapobieganie szkodom lub zagrożeniom. - Model jakości w użytkowaniu (Quality in use): obejmuje m.in. łagodzenie ryzyka etycznego i społecznego (w obszarach takich jak sprawiedliwość, rozliczalność, prywatność i kontrola człowieka). Próba zwizualizowania obu standardów mogłaby wyglądać jak poniżej. Chcesz przełożyć te standardy na praktykę? W ramach akcji Black Box November możesz teraz zapisać się na wybrane szkolenia z obszaru AI i testowania w niższych cenach. Sprawdź dostępne terminy i programy na stronie promocji.

title: Ladybird's first alpha release
text: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
text: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. title: A Slinky on an Escalator Is a Weirdly Good Test of LLM Intelligence
author: reddmachine
text: Slinky Escalator Benchmark: 15 Models By Nishaanth Reddy · I started this as a follow-up to the pelican-on-a-bicycle test, pushed toward inter-object physics. Every time a new model drops, I ask it for a single HTML file of a rainbow slinky walking down an up escalator forever, with real physics instead of a scripted animation. Fifteen models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have tried it so far. It’s a silly test, though it’s turned into a surprisingly good gut-check for how capable these models actually are. Getting a slinky to flip down moving steps without stalling or flying off takes spring physics, step collisions and enough self-testing to spot when the result looks off. [00] The Prompt Each model gets this exact prompt once in an empty folder, with no follow-ups or manual edits. I set reasoning effort to xhigh, or high when the agent doesn’t offer xhigh. Make a single HTML file of a rainbow slinky walking down an up escalator, in perpetual motion. Make it realistic and not a scripted animation. Have a start, stop and reset button. setup: agents, effort, recording Slinky on an up escalator: setup Prompt (paste once): Make a single HTML file of a rainbow slinky walking down an up escalator, in perpetual motion. Make it realistic and not a scripted animation. Have a start, stop and reset button. Rules - One fresh, empty folder per model. - Reasoning effort xhigh, or high where the agent doesn't offer xhigh. - Send the prompt once. No follow-ups and no edits to the output. - Build time runs from sending the prompt to the agent's final answer. Agents as run - Codex CLI 0.167.0 and 0.169.1: model_reasoning_effort = "xhigh" - Claude Code 2.1.322: /effort xhigh - Antigravity CLI 1.5.10: --effort xhigh, or high where xhigh is not offered Recording - Chromium at 1280 x 720 with 2x to 3x pixel density. - A fixed 60 Hz virtual clock drives requestAnimationFrame and performance.now. - Press Start, let it run 0.2 s, then capture 20 s, cropped to the slinky. [01] The Runs Click any two clips below to compare them. Even with “not a scripted animation” in the prompt, several models still bend the rules to keep the slinky going. A few adjust the escalator speed to hold it in frame. Others add a small torque assist or reset the slinky if it stalls. These are single runs across three different agents (Codex CLI, Claude Code and Antigravity CLI), recorded on a virtual 60 Hz clock so heavy sims don’t drop frames. It’s purely an anecdotal check. API cost is what each run’s tokens would have cost at that day’s API prices, though I ran all of these on subscription plans. Both pages that came out of this first prompt were guided animations, so the November prompt asks for realistic, unscripted physics instead. Left: GPT-6 Astra, max effort, Codex CLI. Right: Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Code. The video labels both sides "max". The Claude session most likely ran at xhigh.
